items.title: DSA kya hai aur interview mein kaise use hota hai
items.one_idea: DSA is two things, a data structure (how data is organised) and an algorithm (the steps that use it), and an interview checks whether your steps still work when the data is huge: 10 lakh sorted names take up to 1,000,000 checks one by one but about 20 with halving.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ने पूछा: 10 लाख names में एक name, 20 steps में कैसे ढूँढोगे?

items.title: Big-O: steps ka growth, seconds nahi
items.one_idea: Big-O says how the number of steps grows when the input grows: one-by-one search grows in step with the data (10 lakh to 20 lakh names is 10 lakh to 20 lakh steps), halving adds one step, checking every pair quadruples when data doubles.

items.title: Space complexity: memory dekar time bachana
items.one_idea: Space complexity says how much extra memory an algorithm needs as the input grows, and the time-space trade-off is paying memory to save steps: finding a duplicate among 10 lakh numbers takes about 5 hundred billion pair checks with no extra memory, but 10 lakh steps if you spend memory on a set.
items.spoken_hook: Code अटक रहा था, memory बढ़ाते ही चल गया।
items.visual_idea: Two lanes: pair lines vs a set shelf; step and memory bars swap sizes.
items.everyday_anchor: A shopkeeper who keeps a price list on the wall instead of recalculating every price at the counter.
items.example: EXAMPLE (ran it, Python 3.12, counts not seconds): n(n-1)/2 = 499999500000 pair checks for 10 lakh ints (n=1000: 499500; n=2000: 1999000); set: 1000000 steps; getsizeof list 8000056 B vs set 33554648 B = about 4x (container only).
facts_to_verify: Do not claim set lookup is O(1) as a Python fact.
Show real printed counts; no exact bytes or seconds on screen.
Say the set costs O(n) to build and O(n) memory.

items.title: Arrays: memory mein kaise rakhe jaate hain
items.one_idea: An array keeps its elements in one unbroken block of memory, each the same size, so the computer finds element i with one calculation (start + i x size), which makes reading any element one step, while inserting in the middle must shift every element after it (about 5 lakh moves in a 10 lakh array).
items.spoken_hook: Array में दस लाखवाँ element, एक step में कैसे?
items.hook_source: direct_question is the one of the five types not yet tested; hookscore 30.0 WEAK (Hinglish), no DEALBREAKER.
items.visual_idea: A long row of equal memory boxes with offsets 0, 4, 8 ... and a pointer jumping straight to box 999,999 by one multiplication while a crawling magnifier is crossed out; then a new value inserted in the middle makes the boxes after it slide right with a move counter reaching 5,00,000.
items.everyday_anchor: Cinema hall seats numbered in order: seat 40 is found by counting, not searching; squeezing one person into the middle moves everyone after them.
items.example: EXAMPLE (strategist ran it, researcher re-ran it 2026-10-22, Python 3.12, counts not seconds): array('i') of 1000000 ints: itemsize 4 bytes; byte offset of index 0 is 0, 1 is 4, 2 is 8, 999999 is 3999996; inserting in the middle of 1000000 items shifts 500000, of 2000000 shifts 1000000. 4 bytes is this machine's itemsize; say 'for example 4 bytes'.
facts_to_verify: Confirmed by researcher 2026-10-22. Do not claim Python list internals, real addresses, or seconds. Say 'inserting makes the elements after it move'.

items.title: Strings: array jaisi, par badal nahi sakte
items.one_idea: A string is a row of characters you read by index from 0 like an array, but in Python it is immutable (a character cannot be changed in place; a change makes a brand-new string), so building a long string with + in a loop copies the growing string every time (model: 1000 appends copy 500500 characters, 10 lakh appends about 5 hundred billion) while one join copies each character once.
items.spoken_hook: String का एक letter बदलने गया, तो error क्यों आया?
items.hook_source: wrong_way_first is the untested formula of the five-type set: company_specific has no fetched interview page (the Oracle Java docs page only says Java strings are constant), so the best untested variant is the tempting wrong way (s[0]='j') failing for real. Plain words only, no unexplained term; the next line teaches at once. Hookscore pending the scriptwriter (Hinglish lines score low; only a DEALBREAKER matters).
items.hook_10s: String का एक letter बदलने गया, error आ गया। मान लो s = "hello" है। s[0] में "j" लिखो, तो Python बोलता है TypeError: string में item assignment नहीं होता। [frame 0: five letter boxes h e l l o numbered 0 to 4, a pencil on box 0 with a red cross and the real error line under it]

items.visual_idea: Five touching letter boxes h e l l o with index 0 to 4 under them, a pointer jumping straight to box 4 to read it; a pencil swinging at box 0 is blocked with a red cross and the real error line; then a NEW row j e l l o is drawn beside the old row (old row stays) to show a change makes a copy; then a staircase of rows growing one letter at a time, each step re-copying the whole row with a copy counter climbing to 500500 for 1000 appends, against one single row filled left to right with a counter of 1000.
items.everyday_anchor: A printed wedding card: a typo cannot be fixed on the card, you reprint a whole new card; reprinting the full card for every added name is slow, so you collect all the names and print once.
items.example: EXAMPLE (researcher ran it 2026-10-23, Python 3.12.3, counts not seconds): s='hello'; s[0] is 'h', s[4] is 'o'; s[0]='j' raises TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment; 'j'+s[1:] gives 'jello' as a new string. Copy-count MODEL (each + copies the whole current string, n(n+1)/2): n=1000 -> 500500 vs join 1000; n=100000 -> 5000050000 vs 100000; n=1000000 -> 500000500000 vs 1000000. It is a model, not a measured CPython time.
facts_to_verify: Confirmed by researcher 2026-10-23: Python docs call str an immutable sequence of Unicode code points; Wikipedia says strings are typically implemented as arrays (say 'often an array' and 'sequence indexed from 0 like an array'); never say Python stores a str as an array.

Python FAQ gives two reasons for immutability: storage fixed at creation (performance) and strings as elemental as numbers. Do NOT say the FAQ says it is for dict keys; the hash-must-not-change point is from the datamodel page and is optional.

stdtypes docs: repeated concatenation of immutable sequences has quadratic runtime cost, use str.join. Do NOT claim CPython's += optimisation exists or not, slice cost, memory layout, UTF-8 vs fixed width, ids.
Label every immutability statement 'in Python'; Java strings are also constant (Java docs); other languages differ, so never say 'all languages'.
Copy counts are a labelled model (EXAMPLE pill); the builder re-runs the code and shows the real printed output; no seconds on screen.
Numbers spoken in Hindi words with braces, e.g. 10{दस} लाख, 500{पाँच सौ} अरब; the hook has no unexplained term.
